opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most important questions, and it's one that often gets lost in the excitement around AI for drug discovery. There's a tendency to treat discovery as the bottleneck, as if once you've identified a promising molecule or a candidate antigen, the hard part is over. But in reality, discovery is only the very front end of a long and expensive pipeline. You still have preclinical work, toxicology, formulation, multiple phases of clinical trials, regulatory review, manufacturing scale-up, distribution, and then actually getting the countermeasure into people's arms or hands. And historically, most of the cost and most of the time sits in those later stages, not in discovery.

So if AI investment focuses only on accelerating discovery, you can end up in a situation where you've got a much bigger pile of candidates sitting at the entrance to a pipeline that hasn't gotten any wider. That doesn't necessarily make us safer. In the worst case it just shifts the bottleneck downstream.

What I'd like to see is investment that looks at the whole value chain. That means asking where AI can genuinely help with things like predicting toxicity earlier so we fail fewer candidates in expensive late-stage trials, designing smarter and more adaptive trials, improving manufacturing processes so we can scale production quickly, and supporting regulators so they can evaluate evidence faster without cutting corners on safety. It also means investing in the non-AI parts: manufacturing capacity, trial networks that are ready to go before an emergency hits, and the institutional arrangements that let countries share data and doses fairly.

There's also a security dimension here that I think is underappreciated. The same capabilities that make it easier to design a therapeutic can, in some cases, lower barriers to designing something harmful. So if we're making the offensive side of the equation cheaper and faster, we need to make sure the defensive side, the whole process of getting a countermeasure from idea to deployment, is getting faster too. Otherwise the gap between threat and response actually widens.

So my short answer is: don't treat AI as a magic wand you wave at the discovery stage. Treat it as one tool among many, and fund the end-to-end system so that a good idea can actually become a medicine that reaches people when they need it.

r001.rationale: It says downstream stages take most of the time and cost, but gives no roughly decade-long timeline or instantaneous-discovery scenario.

r002.rationale: It does not mention decades of prior mRNA vaccine development or how that limits replicating COVID-era vaccine speed.

r003.rationale: It recommends funding the whole value chain and accelerating downstream steps such as trials, manufacturing scale-up, regulatory review, and deployment.

r004.rationale: It discusses safety and security but does not say people, rather than AI systems, must be accountable for downstream harms.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the field has been seduced by the front end of the pipeline. Discovery is where the exciting demos live. You get a model that proposes a novel antibiotic scaffold or predicts a protein structure, and it makes a wonderful headline. But discovery is maybe the first ten or fifteen percent of the journey. The thing that actually saves lives is a vial on a shelf, in a stockpile, with a regulatory approval behind it and a supply chain that can scale it when a pathogen shows up. And almost none of the AI investment has gone to that part.

So when I think about where capital should go, I'd break it into roughly three bottlenecks after discovery. The first is preclinical and translational work. Toxicology, pharmacokinetics, formulation, picking a dose. This is slow, expensive, and heavily empirical, and it's where most candidates die. AI can help here, but only if people invest in the data infrastructure, because the datasets are fragmented, proprietary, and often just not digitised. You can't train your way out of a problem where the data doesn't exist. So some of the money has to go into generating and sharing boring data, which is a very hard sell to investors.

The second bottleneck is clinical and regulatory. For medical countermeasures specifically, this is peculiar, because for many threats you cannot run a traditional efficacy trial. You're not going to deliberately expose people to a filovirus. So you rely on animal models, biomarkers, correlates of protection, and things like the FDA Animal Rule. AI could make a real contribution in building better predictive models of human response from animal and in vitro data, and in helping regulators reason about evidence under uncertainty. But that requires regulators to be at the table early, resourced, and willing to engage with these tools. If you build an AI system that produces evidence the regulator cannot interpret or trust, you've built nothing.

The third is manufacturing and deployment, which is almost entirely neglected. Process development, scale-up, quality control, cold chain, distribution. Think about how many of the COVID-era delays were not about having a candidate but about producing it at volume and getting it to people. There's a lot of room for AI in process optimisation, in predicting batch failures, in planning stockpiles against threat scenarios. It's unglamorous, but if you want a countermeasure to actually be a countermeasure, this is where you need to spend.

And then underneath all of that there's a coordination problem. The market for medical countermeasures is broken in a well-understood way. Nobody wants to buy an anthrax antitoxin until there's anthrax. So the incentives for private AI investment to go downstream are weak, and that argues for public and philanthropic capital taking on end-to-end responsibility rather than funding another discovery platform and hoping the rest sorts itself out. I'd like to see funders commit to the whole arc for a handful of priority threats, with AI integrated at each stage, rather than scattering money across a hundred discovery startups.

The last thing I'd add is a cautionary note. The same tools that compress discovery timelines can, in principle, lower the barrier for someone trying to cause harm. So part of a mature investment strategy is building in biosecurity safeguards and governance from the start, not bolting them on afterwards. If we get the full pipeline right, we get faster, more resilient responses to pandemics and to deliberate threats. If we only do the discovery part, we get impressive papers and empty shelves.

r001.rationale: The response says discovery is only the first ten or fifteen percent of the journey, but does not state that instantaneous discovery could still leave roughly a decade before patient access.

r002.rationale: It does not mention decades of prior mRNA vaccine development or how that history limits replication of COVID-era speed.

r003.rationale: It recommends investing across post-discovery bottlenecks, including preclinical and translational work, clinical and regulatory processes, and manufacturing and deployment.

r004.rationale: It calls for biosecurity safeguards and governance, but does not say that people must be accountable for potential downstream harms from approved countermeasures.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to look at the whole pathway, from discovering a promising molecule to getting a safe, effective product to the people who need it. Drug discovery is an important part of that, but it’s only one part. You still have to establish whether the candidate works, evaluate its safety, run clinical trials, manufacture it reliably, and distribute it.

If AI investment concentrates on discovery, we could end up generating many more candidates without increasing our capacity to evaluate or produce them. We’ve accelerated one stage, but the bottleneck has simply moved downstream.

So I’d want that investment to be guided by where it can actually shorten the time to an available medical countermeasure. That might include better tools for designing trials or developing manufacturing processes, alongside investment in the laboratories, facilities, and people needed to carry out that work. AI doesn’t substitute for those capabilities.

The measure of success should be whether we can deliver a countermeasure safely, quickly, and at the scale required—not simply how many promising molecules we can identify.

r001.rationale: The response says downstream steps can remain bottlenecks, but it does not mention instantaneous discovery or a roughly decade-long delay to patient access.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss mRNA vaccine development history or limits on replicating COVID-era speed.

r003.rationale: It recommends investing in steps after discovery, including trial-design tools, manufacturing processes, and the facilities and people needed to deliver countermeasures.

r004.rationale: It does not address accountability for downstream harms or say that responsibility must rest with people rather than AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to look at the whole pathway, rather than just the discovery step. Finding a promising molecule is valuable, but it doesn’t mean you have a safe, effective medical countermeasure that you can manufacture at scale and get to the people who need it.

So investment in AI should also address the bottlenecks downstream: preclinical testing, clinical trials, regulatory review, manufacturing, and distribution. If you accelerate discovery enormously but leave all of those other stages unchanged, you may just create a longer queue of candidates waiting to be tested.

And that means working with the people responsible for each stage early on. What evidence will regulators need? Can this product actually be manufactured? How will it be delivered in the settings where it’s needed? The measure of success should ultimately be whether we can get an effective intervention to people faster, rather than simply how many molecules we can generate.

r001.rationale: It says unchanged downstream stages could create a queue, but gives no roughly decade-long estimate or explicit patient-access timeline.

r002.rationale: It does not mention mRNA vaccine development history or a head start limiting replication of COVID-era speed.

r003.rationale: It explicitly recommends investing in downstream bottlenecks, including preclinical testing, trials, regulatory review, manufacturing, and distribution.

r004.rationale: It does not address accountability for downstream harms or state that people, rather than AI systems, must bear it.
